title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for LNG | Dye Penetrant (US)
description: On-site liquid penetrant testing for US LNG plants: stainless piping, nickel steel and aluminum welds with controlled penetrant materials. Request a quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for LNG Facilities in the United States
html:
Liquid penetrant testing (PT), also called dye penetrant inspection, is the surface method that works on every metal in an LNG plant: austenitic stainless piping, nickel-alloy and 9% nickel steel welds, aluminum exchanger nozzles and carbon steel alike. Atlantis mobilizes qualified technicians across the United States to examine welds, repairs and machined surfaces for flaws open to the surface. To scope a job, request a PT inspection quote and attach the weld map or isometrics.

Why penetrant carries so much of the LNG surface-inspection load

The cold side of an LNG plant is built from metals that magnetic particle testing cannot examine. Cryogenic process piping is 304L or 316L stainless, which is nonmagnetic, and the large heat exchangers are aluminum. Penetrant testing does not depend on magnetism. It depends on liquid wicking into a flaw that is open to the surface, then being drawn back out by a developer so the flaw shows as a bright line or dot. That makes PT the default surface check for the finished welds of cryogenic piping, vessel nozzles, tank-to-pipe connections and repairs, whatever the alloy.

The trade-off is that PT finds only flaws that break the surface. Subsurface lack of fusion and internal porosity are invisible to it, so a complete cryogenic weld plan pairs PT with ultrasonic testing for LNG or volumetric methods that the owner arranges. Where steel is magnetic, magnetic particle testing for LNG may be faster, and the pages explain how to choose.

US requirements behind LNG penetrant work

Onshore LNG plants fall under PHMSA 49 CFR Part 193, which incorporates NFPA 59A. Export and import terminals are authorized by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, with Coast Guard oversight of marine transfer. Construction codes then define what must be examined: ASME B31.3 for process piping, ASME Section VIII for pressure vessels, API 620 and API 625 for tanks. The examination method follows ASME Section V Article 6, and ASTM E165 is the common practice standard. Acceptance is set by the construction code, typically as limits on linear and rounded indications. The owner's inspector decides acceptance; we record and report.

Penetrant materials and contamination limits

Austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys are sensitive to the chemistry of the materials applied to them. Halogens, particularly chlorides, and sulfur in penetrants, cleaners and developers can contribute to cracking in service or at elevated temperature. Article 6 therefore requires that penetrant materials used on these alloys be controlled for halogen and sulfur content, and users must keep batch certifications on file. Atlantis uses the material family and lot records the procedure names, and retains the certification for the owner's quality file.

The same concern applies to cleaners. A solvent that leaves residue can plug a crack and give a false clean result, and rough or smeared surfaces from grinding, peening or wire brushing can close flaws. The procedure therefore specifies cleaning before examination and, on stainless, avoids steel wire brushes that would embed carbon. After testing, penetrant and developer residue is removed so it cannot contaminate liquefaction systems or interfere with coatings.

Technique choices for LNG welds

Penetrant technique selection for LNG components
SituationTypical techniqueReason
Field welds on stainless pipe racksVisible, solvent-removable penetrant with solvent-based developerPortable, no water or darkening needed
Shop welds on nozzles and spoolsFluorescent penetrant where lighting is controlledHigher sensitivity on tight, fine flaws
9% nickel steel repairsVisible penetrant, as an alternative to magnetizingAvoids residual magnetism
Aluminum exchanger nozzle weldsLow-contamination visible penetrantNonmagnetic metal; surface cleanliness is critical
Cold or frosted surfacesWarm and dry the area, or use a qualified low-temperature procedurePenetrant does not work reliably on wet or frozen surfaces

How the penetrant examination is performed

After precleaning and drying, the penetrant is applied and left for the dwell time set in the procedure, which depends on the material, the flaw type sought and the temperature. Excess is removed with the method the procedure specifies, a solvent-dampened wipe for solvent-removable systems, taking care not to flood the surface and wash out shallow flaws. A thin, even layer of developer is applied, and the part is examined within the developing time window under adequate white light, or under a black light in a darkened area for fluorescent systems.

The technician classifies each indication as relevant or nonrelevant, measures it, and records it with a sketch or photograph. A bleed-out that grows after the developing window is tracked separately, because long bleed can indicate a tight crack rather than porosity. Where the code allows, indications are dressed or removed and the area is re-tested after the repair; the original and re-test results are both reported.

Temperature and surface limits

Standard penetrant techniques are qualified for a surface temperature range. Cold lines in operation, or a tank skin on a winter morning, can fall outside it, and heated surfaces can flash off the penetrant before it works. We confirm the temperature at the quote stage, and where it is outside the standard range the procedure is qualified at the actual temperature, or the work waits for the surface to be brought into range. Insulated cold piping is tested at the windows the owner opens and in the dry, not in condensation or while frost is forming.

When in the weld sequence penetrant is applied

Penetrant testing on LNG work happens at several stages, not only at the end. On thick-wall stainless and nickel-alloy joints, an interpass check after grinding the root or a hot-pass surface can catch a crack before more weld metal buries it, and the repair is then a small grind rather than a cut-out. A final PT of the completed surface, after cleaning and any required passivation steps, documents the finished joint. Repairs get their own check after excavation to confirm the flaw is gone and again after re-welding. Each of these steps appears as a line in the report, so the weld history is traceable by date and procedure.

Flaws penetrant finds in cryogenic fabrication

Austenitic stainless welds develop hot cracks and crater cracks, particularly at stops and restarts and in fully austenitic filler. Nickel-alloy welds are prone to microfissures and solidification cracking if heat input and cleanliness are poorly controlled. Aluminum exchanger welds show porosity and lack of fusion at the surface, and arc strikes and grinding gouges on any metal can start fatigue cracks that grow under thermal cycling. Penetrant displays these as sharp, continuous lines for cracks and as scattered round dots for porosity, and an experienced Level II tells them apart by how the bleed-out develops over the developing time.

False indications come from rough surfaces, scale, weld spatter, and incomplete removal of excess penetrant. A technician who sees a suspicious bleed-out recleans and retests the spot rather than reporting it as a crack, and the report distinguishes confirmed flaws from false indications resolved by retest.

Surface preparation before penetrant goes on

Penetrant can only enter a flaw that is clean and open. Paint, mill scale, oxide and oil have to come off the weld and a band of base metal beside it, and the preparation method must not smear metal across the surface. On stainless and nickel alloys, grinding with dedicated, iron-free abrasives avoids cross-contamination, and mechanical cleaning that peens or burnishes the surface is followed by a light etch or other treatment where the procedure requires it. After precleaning, the surface must be dry; solvent trapped in a crack will keep penetrant out, so the procedure sets a drying time before application.

What the PT report contains

  • Component ID, weld number, drawing reference and material, with location
  • Procedure number and revision, the code of record and the acceptance criteria
  • Penetrant, remover and developer type and batch numbers, with halogen and sulfur certifications for stainless and nickel alloys
  • Surface temperature, precleaning method, dwell and developing times
  • Technician name and SNT-TC-1A level, and the Level III who approved the procedure
  • Indications with location, length and type, photographs or sketches, and accept or reject against the named criteria

What to send for a PT quote

  • Weld maps or isometrics, the number of joints and their material, size and thickness
  • Code, specification and acceptance criteria
  • Surface condition, coating and insulation status, and who prepares the surface
  • Operating or ambient temperature of the surfaces at the time of testing
  • Requirement for chloride or sulfur certification of the penetrant materials
  • Site address, permits, TWIC and access arrangements

Planning for US LNG sites

Penetrant materials are flammable solvents, so hot-work and ignition-source controls apply, and many areas of an LNG plant are classified. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope and bring pre-certified consumables, but the owner arranges site orientation, gas monitoring, permits and the access for the work. Shutdowns are short and crowded; PT is sequenced after grinding and fit-up and before insulation, coating or hydrotest. Gulf Coast humidity and rain interrupt the work, so a tent or enclosure on exposed pipe racks keeps the schedule intact.

Training your own PT technicians

Teams that want in-house capacity can take PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training and practice on the penetrant testing simulator. The employer certifies its personnel under its written practice. Procedure development and qualification are part of procedure qualification and demonstration.

What we do not do

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, does not run in-line inspection tools and does not offer specialist techniques outside MT, PT and UT. We do not decide acceptance or repair on your behalf, and we do not calculate remaining life; those decisions belong to the owner's inspector or engineer using our report.

faq.q: Is penetrant testing the right method for stainless steel LNG piping?
faq.a: Yes for surface-breaking flaws on the finished weld surface, because stainless is nonmagnetic and MT cannot be used. It does not see internal flaws, so most specifications pair it with ultrasonic or volumetric examination.

faq.q: Do penetrant materials need special certification on stainless and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Yes. ASME Section V Article 6 requires control of halogen and sulfur content in materials used on austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys, and we keep batch certifications and list them in the report.

faq.q: Can PT be done on cold or frosty LNG surfaces?
faq.a: Not reliably. Moisture and ice block penetrant entry, and low temperatures slow it. The surface is warmed and dried, or the procedure is qualified for the actual temperature before testing.

faq.q: Why use PT instead of MT on 9% nickel steel?
faq.a: MT is possible on 9% nickel steel but can leave residual magnetism that disrupts later welding. PT avoids the issue entirely, so many owners choose it for final surface checks and repairs on nickel steel.

faq.q: What codes apply to PT at a US LNG terminal?
faq.a: PHMSA 49 CFR Part 193 and NFPA 59A set the framework, API 620 and API 625 cover tanks, and ASME B31.3 covers piping. ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165 govern the method.

faq.q: How do you handle residue after testing?
faq.a: Penetrant and developer are removed with the cleaning method in the procedure so they cannot contaminate cryogenic or process systems or interfere with coatings. The cleaning step is recorded in the report.

faq.q: Who decides whether an indication is rejectable?
faq.a: Our Level II technician evaluates each indication against the named acceptance criteria and reports it, and the owner's inspector or engineer makes the acceptance and repair decision. A Level III approves the procedure.

faq.q: What do you need to quote an LNG penetrant job?
faq.a: Weld maps or isometrics, materials, thicknesses, joint count, code and acceptance criteria, surface temperature, coating and insulation status, any chloride and sulfur certification requirement, site address and access details.

faq.q: Is radiography part of an LNG weld scope with Atlantis?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States because industrial radiography requires licensing under federal or state radiation rules. We handle PT, MT and UT and can work alongside your licensed contractor.
